newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - Powerscreen sees continued growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Powerscreen sees continued growth.

text.p: Northern Ireland-based engineering group Powerscreen International Plc said on Wednesday it was comfortable with analysts' forecasts predicting pre-tax profits of 47.5-48.5 million stg in the current financial year.
Powerscreen reported pre-tax profits of 42.4 million stg in the year to end-March 1997, up from 36.0 million the previous year, and said the current year would follow the same market trends.
"If you look at broker analysis for what is going to happen in the current year, they're looking at the 47.5-48.5 million range for profits," finance director Barry Cosgrove told Reuters.
"We're not unhappy with that at this stage, we have a good order book right across the group."
Cosgrove said Powerscreen was achieving good growth in spite of weak conditions in continental Europe and the strength of sterling.
"We don't see any upturn in the German market at all," he said. "But we are strong in other markets and we are able to grow despite conditions in Europe."
He said the strength of sterling had reduced Powerscreen's annual profits by about 1.1 million stg in the year to end-March.

"Because we sell in sterling, it's very difficult to know what the exchange impact is," he said. "The European market was very tough for us last year but we can't be sure how much of that was exchange and how much was economic weakness in the German market."

Cosgrove said Powerscreen aimed to continue expanding its sales in the Far East, South Africa and South America. But he said there were no plans to set up manufacturing facilities or make acquisitions in these areas in the foreseeable future.
In a statement which accompanied Powerscreen's results, chairman John Craig forecast a strong year in markets outside Europe.

"In many respects Powerscreen expects the current year to follow last year's market trends," he said. "Powerscreen believes it will have a strong year in North America, UK/Ireland and the Far East. Europe we see as still providing the hardest challenge because of overall economic conditions."
